entries.meaning: A small bag a woman carries money and personal things in. ---
examples: She dug through her purse looking for her keys.
Someone grabbed her purse right off the back of the chair.
All the purses on that rack are half off.
entries.contrast: In American English a purse is what the British call a handbag; a British purse is a small wallet for coins.

entries.meaning: A woman's bag for keys, money, and small personal items. ---
examples: She set her handbag down on the counter and forgot it.
The store sells shoes and handbags on the second floor.
That designer handbag costs more than my rent.

entries.meaning: A bag carried on your back with two shoulder straps. ---
examples: He threw his backpack in the back seat and got in.
The kids' backpacks are lined up by the front door.
My laptop fits in the front pocket of my backpack.
entries.contrast: Americans say backpack; the British usually say rucksack.

entries.meaning: A stiff rectangular case for carrying clothes when you travel. ---
examples: My suitcase was the last one off the belt.
We packed two suitcases for a week in Florida.
The airline lost his suitcase somewhere in Denver.

entries.meaning: A flat case for carrying papers and a laptop to work. ---
examples: He still carries the leather briefcase he got in law school.
She snapped her briefcase shut and stood up.
The bins were full of laptops and briefcases.

entries.meaning: A small folding case for cards and paper money. ---
examples: I left my wallet in my other jacket.
He pulled an old photo out of his wallet.
Somebody stole two wallets out of the locker room.

entries.meaning: A large open bag with two handles, usually cloth. ---
examples: She keeps a canvas tote bag in the car for groceries.
The museum was handing out free tote bags.
Everything I need for the beach fits in one tote bag.

entries.meaning: A small soft bag that closes at the top. ---
examples: The camera came with a padded pouch.
She keeps her makeup in a little zip pouch.
There are two mesh pouches inside the lid.

entries.meaning: A stiff shoulder bag with a flap that folds over the top. ---
examples: He wore a beat-up leather satchel across his chest.
Her books barely fit in that satchel.
The shop sells handmade satchels.

entries.meaning: A long soft cylindrical bag for clothes or gym gear. ---
examples: He shoved everything into a duffel bag and left.
Two duffel bags were already in the trunk.
My gym clothes live in a duffel bag in the car.
entries.contrast: Also spelled duffle; the two spellings sound exactly the same.

entries.meaning: A small bag worn on a strap around the waist. ---
examples: He wore a fanny pack the whole trip and didn't care.
Fanny packs are apparently back in style.
Keep your passport in the fanny pack, not your pocket.
entries.contrast: American only — the British call it a bum bag, and the word fanny is vulgar in the UK.

entries.meaning: A small bag you take with you into the cabin of a plane. ---
examples: I only travel with a carry-on.
Your carry-on has to fit under the seat in front of you.
They charge extra for carry-ons on that airline now.

entries.meaning: A circular band of metal worn on a finger. ---
examples: She still wears her grandmother's ring.
He lost his wedding ring at the beach.
The case was full of cheap silver rings.

entries.meaning: A chain or string of beads worn around the neck. ---
examples: He gave her a pearl necklace for their anniversary.
The clasp on my necklace keeps coming undone.
She had three thin gold necklaces on at once.
entries.contrast: The ending is unstressed and sounds like -lus, not like the word lace.

entries.meaning: A band or chain worn around the wrist. ---
examples: She wears a thin silver bracelet on her left wrist.
The bracelet was a gift from her sister.
He bought two beaded bracelets at the market.

entries.meaning: A piece of jewelry worn in or on the ear. ---
examples: I lost one earring somewhere in the car.
She has small gold earrings in today.
Those earrings are way too heavy for me.

entries.meaning: An ornament that hangs from a chain around the neck. ---
examples: The chain holds a small silver pendant.
She never takes the pendant off, even to swim.
The case had a row of jade pendants.

entries.meaning: A decorative pin fastened to clothing. ---
examples: She pinned a brooch to her collar.
The brooch belonged to his grandmother.
Antique brooches sell well at that shop.
entries.contrast: Spelled with oo but pronounced to rhyme with coach.

entries.meaning: A small case on a chain that opens to hold a photo. ---
examples: There's a tiny photo of her dad inside the locket.
She wore a heart-shaped locket every single day.
That shop repairs old lockets.

entries.meaning: A line of connected metal links worn as jewelry. ---
examples: He wears a thick gold chain under his shirt.
The chain broke and the pendant fell off.
She keeps both rings on a chain around her neck.

entries.meaning: A small ball with a hole through it, strung to make jewelry. ---
examples: One bead rolled under the couch and disappeared.
The dress is covered in tiny glass beads.
She strung the beads onto a wire.

entries.meaning: A cut and polished stone used in jewelry. ---
examples: The ring has a small green gem in the center.
He collects rough gems and cuts them himself.
That gem is almost certainly glass.

entries.meaning: A precious stone, or a piece of jewelry containing one. ---
examples: One jewel was missing from the crown.
The jewels were locked in a hotel safe.
She finally sold the last of her mother's jewels.
entries.contrast: Americans write jewelry; the British write jewellery.

entries.meaning: A very hard, clear precious stone. ---
examples: The diamond on her ring is tiny but it's real.
He can't tell diamonds from cubic zirconia.
They set a single diamond in a plain gold band.

entries.meaning: A small round white gem that forms inside an oyster. ---
examples: She wore a single pearl on a thin chain.
My grandmother left me her pearls.
That pearl is cultured, not natural.
entries.contrast: The ea here has the vowel of girl, not the vowel of ear.

entries.meaning: A deep red precious stone. ---
examples: The ring has a dark red ruby set in gold.
He can't afford real rubies.
That ruby came out of a mine in Burma.

entries.meaning: A bright green precious stone. ---
examples: She picked out a ring with a small emerald.
The necklace has emeralds set all the way around.
That emerald has a chip in the corner.

entries.meaning: A blue precious stone. ---
examples: Her engagement ring has a blue sapphire instead of a diamond.
The bracelet is set with tiny sapphires.
He paid way too much for that sapphire.

entries.meaning: A yellow precious metal used for coins and jewelry. ---
examples: The ring is fourteen-karat gold.
She only wears gold, never silver.
The price of gold went up again this week.

entries.meaning: A shiny white precious metal used for jewelry and utensils. ---
examples: The chain is real silver, not plated.
Silver tarnishes if you don't wear it.
She likes silver better than gold.

entries.meaning: A heavy silver-white metal, more expensive than gold. ---
examples: Their wedding bands are platinum.
Platinum costs more than gold right now.
He had the setting made in platinum.

entries.meaning: A hard green stone carved into jewelry and ornaments. ---
examples: She wears a jade bracelet her mother gave her.
The little elephant is carved from jade.
Good jade is not cheap.

entries.meaning: Hard yellow-brown fossilized tree resin used in jewelry. ---
examples: The beads are real amber, not plastic.
There's an insect trapped in that piece of amber.
Amber feels warm against your skin.

entries.meaning: A blue-green stone used in silver jewelry. ---
examples: The ring is silver with a big chunk of turquoise.
She sells turquoise jewelry at the market on weekends.
Real turquoise has dark veins running through it.
entries.contrast: In American English the qu is usually just a k sound: TUR-koyz.

entries.meaning: A single piece of a clear mineral, or the fine cut glass used for good glassware. ---
examples: She hung a crystal in the kitchen window.
The bowl is heavy lead crystal.
He keeps a few quartz crystals on his desk.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The unit of weight used for precious stones. ---
examples: The stone is just under one carat.
The jeweler said it was a full carat.
He has no idea how many carats that ring is.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like carrot; the spelling karat is used for the purity of gold.

entries.meaning: A stiff bracelet that slides over the hand. ---
examples: She wears a stack of gold bangles on one arm.
The bangle slid right off her wrist.
He brought her a silver bangle back from India.

entries.meaning: A chain or band worn around the ankle. ---
examples: She wore a thin gold anklet all summer.
The anklet has a little bell on it.
They sell beaded anklets on the boardwalk.

entries.meaning: A small jeweled crown worn on the front of the head. ---
examples: The little girl refused to take off her plastic tiara.
She wore a tiara at the wedding and pulled it off.
The museum has three antique tiaras on display.

entries.meaning: A circular ornament worn on the head by a king or queen. ---
examples: The crown is a lot heavier than it looks.
Both crowns are behind glass at the museum.
He put a paper crown on his head at dinner.

entries.meaning: A small earring that sits flat against the ear, or a metal knob on clothing. ---
examples: She only wears small diamond studs.
One stud fell out of my ear at the gym.
The jacket has metal studs down both sleeves.

entries.meaning: A large circular earring, or any ring-shaped band. ---
examples: She wore big gold hoops to the party.
One hoop got caught in her scarf.
Small hoops are easier to sleep in.

entries.meaning: A piece of cut glass that imitates a diamond. ---
examples: The jacket is covered in rhinestones.
One rhinestone fell off the strap.
Those aren't diamonds, they're rhinestones.
entries.contrast: The h after the r is silent: RYN-stohn.

entries.meaning: A small clock worn on the wrist or carried in a pocket. ---
examples: My watch is running five minutes fast.
He collects old mechanical watches.
She got a watch for graduation.
entries.contrast: Singular in English even though the Russian часы is plural: one watch, two watches.

entries.meaning: A watch worn on a strap around the wrist. ---
examples: He still wears a wristwatch instead of checking his phone.
The wristwatch was a gift from his wife.
Both wristwatches need new batteries.
entries.contrast: The w in wrist is silent: RIST-wahch.

entries.meaning: A knot with two loops, tied for decoration. ---
examples: She tied a red bow around the box.
The dress has a bow at the waist.
There were paper bows taped to every chair.
entries.contrast: This bow rhymes with go; the bow that means bending forward rhymes with cow.

entries.meaning: A folding cloth canopy on a frame that keeps rain off you. ---
examples: Take an umbrella, it's supposed to rain all afternoon.
The wind turned my umbrella inside out.
There are three broken umbrellas by the door.

entries.meaning: A covering of artificial or real hair worn on the head. ---
examples: She wore a bright red wig to the party.
The wig looked surprisingly real.
The theater keeps a whole rack of wigs backstage.

entries.meaning: A narrow strip of cloth used for tying or decorating. ---
examples: She tied her hair back with a ribbon.
The box came wrapped in gold ribbon.
He saved the ribbons from every present she ever gave him.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A clip that holds hair back on one side of the head. ---
examples: She clipped her bangs back with a barrette.
The barrette snapped in half.
There are barrettes all over the bathroom counter.
entries.contrast: A French borrowing — the stress falls on the second syllable: buh-RET.

entries.meaning: A cloth-covered elastic band for tying hair. ---
examples: She always has a scrunchie on her wrist.
The scrunchie left a crease in her hair.
Scrunchies somehow came back in style.

entries.meaning: A stick used to help you walk. ---
examples: He's been walking with a cane since the surgery.
Her cane is leaning against the chair.
The gift shop downstairs even sells canes.

entries.meaning: A ring or small ornament that holds keys together. ---
examples: She has a little plastic keychain shaped like a cactus.
My keys came off the keychain again.
He collects keychains from every state he visits.

entries.meaning: A cord worn around the neck to hold a badge or keys. ---
examples: Everyone at the conference wore a lanyard.
His badge hangs from a blue lanyard.
They ran out of lanyards at check-in.

entries.meaning: A small card or piece of metal worn to show who you are. ---
examples: You need a badge to get past the front desk.
He flashed his badge and walked right in.
Visitor badges are at the security desk.

entries.meaning: Something like a bag, belt, or scarf worn to complete an outfit. ---
examples: A scarf is the only accessory she ever wears.
The store carries bags, belts, and other accessories.
The right accessory can pull a whole outfit together.
entries.contrast: The cc is pronounced ks: uhk-SES-uh-ree, not uh-SES-uh-ree.

entries.meaning: A small cheap ornament or piece of jewelry. ---
examples: The shelf is covered in trinkets from her travels.
He bought a cheap trinket at the airport.
Most of what's in the box is just trinkets.

entries.meaning: Something you keep or buy to remember a place or an event. ---
examples: She brings back a souvenir from every trip.
The shop is full of overpriced souvenirs.
I kept the ticket stub as a souvenir.
entries.contrast: In American English the stress falls on the last syllable: soo-vuh-NEER.

entries.meaning: A curved piece of glass or plastic that focuses light. ---
examples: One lens popped right out of my glasses.
He wears contact lenses now instead of frames.
The lenses fog up every time I come inside.
entries.contrast: Lens is already singular despite the s on the end; the plural is lenses.

entries.meaning: Colored products put on the face to change how it looks. ---
examples: She doesn't wear much makeup.
He took the stage makeup off with a wipe.
All her makeup is in a bag under the sink.

entries.meaning: Colored wax in a small tube, put on the lips. ---
examples: She put on lipstick in the elevator.
There's lipstick on the rim of the coffee cup.
She has about ten lipsticks in the exact same shade.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A dark cosmetic brushed onto the eyelashes. ---
examples: Her mascara ran halfway through the movie.
I need to buy new mascara.
She never leaves the house without mascara.

entries.meaning: A cosmetic drawn in a line along the edge of the eyelid. ---
examples: She wears heavy black eyeliner.
My eyeliner smudged in the heat.
He borrowed her eyeliner for the show.

entries.meaning: Colored powder or cream put on the eyelids. ---
examples: She dusted on a little gold eyeshadow.
The eyeshadow creased by noon.
That eyeshadow is too dark for daytime.

entries.meaning: Pink or red powder put on the cheeks. ---
examples: She added a little blush to her cheeks.
That blush is way too pink for her.
I ran out of blush two weeks ago.

entries.meaning: Fine dry cosmetic dust patted onto the skin. ---
examples: She set her makeup with translucent powder.
There's powder all over the bathroom counter.
He shook baby powder into his shoes.

entries.meaning: A thick cosmetic used to cover spots and dark circles. ---
examples: A little concealer hides the dark circles.
Her concealer is a shade too light.
I dab concealer under my eyes every morning.

entries.meaning: A sweet-smelling liquid put on the skin. ---
examples: She wears the same perfume her mother wore.
The whole elevator smelled like perfume.
He gave her a bottle of French perfume.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: As a noun the stress is on the first syllable, PUR-fyoom; as a verb it moves to the second, pur-FYOOM.

entries.meaning: A light scented liquid, usually worn by men. ---
examples: He wears way too much cologne.
The bathroom smelled like cheap cologne.
She bought him cologne for his birthday again.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: kuh-LOHN.

entries.meaning: A pleasant smell, or a product made to give one. ---
examples: The brand launched a new fragrance this spring.
This lotion has no added fragrance.
They carry all the major fragrances here.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A product put under the arms to stop body odor. ---
examples: I completely forgot to put on deodorant.
This deodorant doesn't last all day.
Grab some deodorant while you're at the store.

entries.meaning: A cream put on hair after shampoo to soften it. ---
examples: Leave the conditioner in for two minutes.
She uses conditioner every time she washes her hair.
The conditioner bottle is almost empty.

entries.meaning: A thin cream rubbed into the skin. ---
examples: Put some lotion on your hands, they're cracked.
This lotion smells like coconut.
The drugstore had about ten different lotions.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A cream that keeps the skin from drying out. ---
examples: She puts on moisturizer every night.
This moisturizer is too heavy for summer.
Try one of the lighter moisturizers.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: American spelling; the British write moisturiser.

entries.meaning: A cream that protects the skin from burning in the sun. ---
examples: Put on sunscreen before you go out.
The sunscreen washed right off in the water.
He never wears sunscreen and it shows.

entries.meaning: A treatment that cleans, shapes, and paints the fingernails. ---
examples: She got a manicure the day before the wedding.
The manicure lasted about four days.
Manicures are twenty dollars at that place.

entries.meaning: A treatment that cleans, shapes, and paints the toenails. ---
examples: She treats herself to a pedicure once a month.
The pedicure was worth every penny.
They do pedicures in the back room.

entries.meaning: Thin thread used to clean between the teeth. ---
examples: The dentist gave me a free spool of floss.
There's floss in the medicine cabinet.
He owns floss but he never uses it.

entries.meaning: A liquid you rinse your mouth with to clean it. ---
examples: He rinsed with mouthwash on his way out the door.
That mouthwash burns.
We're out of mouthwash again.

entries.meaning: A brush with stiff bristles used on the hair. ---
examples: Have you seen my hairbrush?
The hairbrush is full of hair again.
She keeps two hairbrushes in her bag.

entries.meaning: A sticky liquid sprayed on hair to hold it in place. ---
examples: She went through half a can of hairspray.
The hairspray made his hair crunchy.
Don't use hairspray near an open flame.

entries.meaning: A thick soothing cream, especially for the lips or skin. ---
examples: She keeps lip balm in every coat pocket.
This balm actually helps with chapped lips.
That shop sells handmade balms and soaps.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: The l is silent: BAHM, rhyming with calm.

entries.meaning: Products used on the face and body to improve appearance. ---
examples: She sells cosmetics at a counter in the mall.
The cosmetics aisle is on the left, past the pharmacy.
He's allergic to most cosmetics.
entries.contrast: Used only in the plural — cosmetics, never a cosmetic.

entries.meaning: Everyday items like soap, shampoo, and toothpaste. ---
examples: Pack your toiletries in a separate bag.
The hotel provides basic toiletries.
Security made him throw out half his toiletries.
entries.contrast: Almost always plural — say toiletries, not a toiletry.

entries.meaning: A tool with two blades for cutting hair or nails. ---
examples: He cuts his own hair with clippers.
The nail clippers are in the top drawer.
These clippers need to be oiled.
entries.contrast: Always plural, like scissors: a pair of clippers, never a clipper.

entries.meaning: A small flat case holding face powder and a mirror. ---
examples: She snapped the compact shut and put it away.
The compact has a little mirror inside the lid.
Her purse was full of old compacts.
entries.contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable, KAHM-pakt; the adjective stresses the second, kuhm-PAKT.

entries.meaning: A scented liquid put on the face after shaving.
examples: He splashed on some aftershave and grabbed his keys.
That aftershave smells exactly like my grandfather.
The gift set came with soap and two aftershaves.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
